title: Tyriq Plummer - Scrubbin' Trubble: The Journey to Multiplayer Roguelikery
speaker: Tyriq Plummer
talk_title: Scrubbin' Trubble: The Journey to Multiplayer Roguelikery
description: In this lightning talk, Tyriq will lay out the foundational goals of Scrubbin' Trubble's multiplayer experience - the most ambitious experiment yet in his pursuit of that White Whale "Semi-synchronous Co-operative Multiplayer Turn-Based Roguelike" - and the technical and design challenges faced along the way to realizing those goals (there have been many).

segments.text: TYRIQ: Can you hear me? Good news, everyone. I exist. Today I am going to be talking about
scrubbin trubble which is a game I am working on. This is a lightning talk. There is a lot to talk
about. But hopefully I am definitely not going to be able to get to all of it but hopefully it will
encourage discussion and pique interest. This is a traditional roguelike and traditional-ish
meaning sing rusynchronous and turn base and not real-time. And doesn't make such a big deal about
whose turn it is. Everything exists and operates in the same modality, same space. So the central
con seat of the game is experiment to see if we can make a roguelike that still has the pacing of
a traditional turn-base roguelike but just with multiple players. The other thing that Scrubbin'
Trubble is -- our friend formed Odd Object and wanted to work on something straightforward that
we could use to figure out how the heck a game studio runs. We decided to make this game. The
last thing Scrubbin' trubble is an evolution of something I had a proof of concept of called clean
sweep. And I gave a talk on this. If you want you can check out that talk. Don't do that now,
though, because that would be rude. I am talking. Basically to give an overview, the way that Clean
Sweep worked and handled multiplayers is players could act fully independently and enemies would
act based on which player they were targeting. If an anomie is targeting player one then player two
can move freely. We can have multiple players and enemies coexisting in the same space operating on
their own sort of turn schedule. It was fairly fun with two players. But there were still a
lot of uncertainty, questions that we needed to answer if we wanted to make it into a full game,
and expand it into something commercially viable. Questions we would have had to answer pretty fun
with two players but does it work well with three or more? We did a little testing but
didn't have a ton of it is definitely fun with three or more players. Clean Sweep was
local multiplayer only and I wanted to implement online and I have never done net code before so
that would be a journey. And design things like the awkward inventory management and make it
pretty and more marketable with art. This is the mission for Scrubbin' Trubble. We wanted to retain
turn synchronicity and also make keep it snappy. Sometimes with roguelikes you have to think hard
about what you will do next for quite a long time. And we wanted to keep things more streamlined than
that to keep the pace going. We wanted to have like a streamline easy to use interface. Limited
decision space so players could observe the game field and resolve their actions quickly and have
a clearly readable game state to encourage that and we wanted runs to be relatively quick. This
isn't a huge adventure game. It is really just experiment for the mechanic itself and to that
end we wanted to keep things relatively tight and also just a game that people can hop in
with their friends, you know, n afternoon. Let's do a few ones and call it a day. And to that end,
we wanted to keep the play time relatively short. To achieve all of those, going in,
I knew these were things we would need to have small inventories so you would not to have do
menu diving and be overwhelmed with choice. Distinct and unique enemies. We don't want a
bunch of variance on what does the purple of this enemy do as opposed to the red version.
All that sort of thing. We wanted you to be able to take a quick look at the game state and be
like I know what these things do and I know what my voices are and be able to execute relatively
quickly to keep the game moving along. Similarly, to show threatened enemy zones and actions so you
can be able to make informed decisions quickly. Small stages with explicit goals will help focus
player attention to encourage people sticking close another and working together as opposed
to massive sprawling maps where players go off on their own and it ends feeling like a game where
you might encounter other players. It became apparent we would have to limit overly complex
cascading effects because otherwise that's another reason that the gameplay could really
like come to a stop quickly. Oh, a bunch of stuff just happened, and now we need to parse
all of the things that just occurred. That can be sometimes difficult. These were our goals going
into the game and we started working October 2024 right as Roguelike Celebration 2024 was happening.
Encouraging. A lot of great information. This was imminently useful to the stuff we are going to be
doing. One of the talks was from NecroDancer dev about how they handled net code for the online
version of crypt of the necro dancer. I was like this is perfect. We will copy what they did and
everything is going to be perfectly fine. I spent the next two months banging my head against the
wall trying to figure out how to do rollback code. Again, me never having done net code before, maybe
shouldn't have done that. But it was a little stuff. Ended up not working. Ended up scrapping
it and realizing I guess most online games don't need rollback. That seems like a pretty specific
use case of technology for a pretty specific subset of games. I didn't know that at the
time. Ended up rolling it back to now the game works entirely based in like lock step with the
server. Clients send their action to the server and wait for conformation from the server before
applying events to the game world. Everything is simulated on the client side so the server
doesn't need to send game state. That does mean it is important for us to make sure that the game
operates in a very deterministic way. Internet is just faster than I thought it was. After all this,
finally got internet and Nethack and reimplemented the prototype of Clean Sweep we had in terms of
the way multiplayer worked. All of the questions of does it work for three or more players and how
to keep the pace and stuff up, turns out it just didn't work. The question does this work with 3-4
players that was one of the questions we had and the answer is no. It was too fast, too chaotic,
too unpredictable. The goal was to have it be like players would be able to cooperate
with one another and slow down when they needed to on their own pace. That wasn't a thing that
happened. In order to cooperate, players needed to be constantly talking and telegraphic everyone
of their actions. There was a lot of frequent toe stepping on actions. One player would move while
another player was targeting an enemy that was targeting that player and they would go out of
sync as they confirmed the action. It was a bit of a mess. Fortunately, due to my incredible skill of
crippling self-doubt and not believing in myself, I kind of had a feeling this might be the case.
I had a feeling this might not work out so I had built in a contingency plan where if we needed to
pivot we could. There was a mechanic where players would be able to cue up actions to be executed
simultaneously when another player confirmed their action and we made that the central mechanic as
opposed to auxiliary. Now whenever a player cues up an action, it waits until all players
within the same combat zone all have their actions queued up. I thought this might be the case. It
was a relatively easy pivot to make. But there was a lot of other knock on effects we had to
deal with after that. This also, unfortunately, sort of scrapped one of our initial major goals
which is players will be able to take turns out needing to wait for anybody else. You definitely
need to wait for other players to confirm their turns now. But you only need to do so within a
limited area around you which we call the combat zone. Combat zones defined by who is fighting
who. If you have a player who is in combat or two players who are in combat with a particular enemy
or whatever the case may be, those two players, as long as they are nearby and fighting the same
enemies all mixed together, they will need to wait for each other to confirm actions. If there
is another player off in a different level and not part of that combat they can operate freely
and don't need to wait for anybody. They can just run around. This ended up working better
because now players -- it makes things easier and cooperation easier because you don't need to be
in the constant communication you were before. You can just see what other players are planning to do
and you can still plan more complex scenario but it is a lot easier because the game automatically
slows down when it makes sense to slow down. Here is like a little video example of the way
the game works. You can see the player is moving freely at the start, independently running around,
once they get into the combat, the game stops and waits for everybody to confirm their turns.
You can see here the outlined area is the defined combat zone. Any player outside of that area will
be able to move freely of their own accord not waiting for anybody else. Consequences like I
said it is easier for players to coordinate and combat has definitive start and end points.
You can see the area you are fighting in and when combat ends all the guys are dead or whatever the
case may be and that's the end of combat and you are free to move again which let's us do
fun things like have end of fight quips where we can pop up a close call or if you finish an entire
combat encounter without taking damage you get a score bonus at the end of the level. There are new
hurdles with this such as how do we define combat zones and what are the edge cases? Defining all
these different ways and like OK those players are kind of close enough, should they be in the
same combat zone even though they are fighting different enemies and they are on opposite sides.
Keeping the turn snappy is more important now because you are waiting for other players to
finish their turn. We definitely don't want it to be where one player is resolving what they
need to do in half a second and another player is thinking about stuff for a minute and holding up
the entire combat. A player in a combat zone if they are being targeted by any enemy and try to
involve the least amount of space. You can see the bleacher with the white hat on, and the pod
person to the left is not in that fight. They can move freely but if they get into that area you can
see suddenly they are all in the same zone and the turns are being queued up and waited for and that
sort of thing. There are a couple other things we are going to sort of outside of this just main
sort of gameplay loop we are doing with regards to multiplayer. One of them is players vote on
which stage to go to next. So the way the game works is it takes place all in the same house.
Each level you are going from one room to another selecting which room you want to go to try to keep
the ground. It is a cleaning theme base game. You trying to clean the house and keep the grime in
each room to a certain level so they don't become overrun. Between each level you are voting on
which stage to go to next. There is leveling up and the different leveling up abilities.
Some lean in on the sinner -- synergy. You might take this level of ability and call all our allies
to come close to you before you use a healing potion on yourself so everyone benefits. There is
other ways of healing in the game such as cleaning up other propers you might want other players
nearby for and that sort of thing. And lastly, game overs only occur in the event of a TPK on a
floor. Fallen PCs return on the next floor but if you die, for each player you die, it is a really
big score personality that grows. You still want to not die this being mostly a score-based game
but if you do die, as long as it is not a full party wipe, you will be able to come back on the
next floor and keep playing with your friends, and you can just encourage them from the sidelines.
You can exit levels at any point. If somebody dies and you are in a tough spot, you can leave
the level, take the penalty, and go to the next floor with friends and back in action. I think
I am out of time. That's the end of the talk. There is a lot more I could talk about but --
